summary: This informational document describes where and how IPv6 over constrained-node networks, known as 6lo, can be used. It gives deployment examples across many link technologies, including IEEE 802.15.4, Z-Wave, Bluetooth LE, DECT-ULE, MS/TP, NFC, and power line communication. It is aimed at readers who want to understand and evaluate end-to-end IPv6 on such networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny gadgets like light switches and sensors also want to join the internet. This guide shows the different ways they can, depending on whether they talk by radio, power wire, or touch.

questions: ipv6 over bluetooth le and z-wave
subtitle: Running IPv6 over tiny, low-power devices using different wireless and wired technologies

tldr.problem: Tiny sensor and control devices have limited packet sizes, power budgets, and bandwidth, making standard IPv6 impossible to use directly. Yet these constrained nodes need end-to-end IPv6 connectivity for the Internet of Things to work.
tldr.mechanism: 6lo (IPv6 over constrained-node networks) adapts the 6LoWPAN approach to multiple link-layer technologies, adding packet fragmentation, header compression, address autoconfiguration, and mesh routing adapted to each technology's characteristics.
tldr.outcome: Constrained devices can now participate in IPv6 networks using IEEE 802.15.4, Z-Wave, Bluetooth LE, DECT-ULE, MS/TP, NFC, and power line communication, enabling smart homes, industrial monitoring, smart grids, and wearable healthcare applications.

today: RFC 9453 is an Informational RFC published in September 2023 that describes the applicability of 6lo technologies. It is not obsoleted or updated. The document serves as a guide for engineers evaluating IPv6 over constrained-node networks and documents the real-world deployment landscape of 6lo technologies used in smart grids, smart homes, building automation, and wearable health monitoring systems worldwide.

sections.title: IPv6 for Constrained Devices
sections.content:
IPv6 specifies a minimum MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) of 1,280 octets, but many wireless link-layer technologies used in constrained-node networks support much smaller frames. IEEE 802.15.4 variants typically offer only 127 octets of frame size, and these technologies provide no fragmentation or reassembly. Additionally, IPv6 headers are large, and sending full headers over low-bandwidth links wastes precious power and spectrum. Constrained devices may run on batteries for years and have limited processing power for complex protocol stacks.

The IETF IPv6 over Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Network (6LoWPAN) Working Group created a suite of specifications providing an adaptation layer that sits between IPv6 and the link layer. This layer performs fragmentation and reassembly, packet header compression, address autoconfiguration, and neighbor discovery optimization. As IoT deployments expanded beyond 802.15.4 to other link-layer technologies—Bluetooth LE, Z-Wave, power line communication, and others—the IETF created "6lo" to apply 6LoWPAN techniques to these technologies. This document provides applicability guidance for engineers evaluating 6lo for their constrained-node networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets need IPv6 to talk to the Internet, but IPv6 sends very big packets. The solution is to squish the packets down, send them slowly, and glue them back together on the other end.

sections.title: 6lo Link-Layer Technologies and Comparison
sections.content:
6lo encompasses adaptation layers for seven major link-layer technologies. ITU-T G.9959 (Z-Wave) is a short-range narrowband radio technology used for smart home automation with mesh networking at layer 2, supporting transmission ranges up to 100 meters per hop. Bluetooth LE, supported by most smartphones and wearables, operates at 1-2 Mbps with 100-meter outdoor range and is evolving to support mesh networking. DECT-ULE is a low-power variant of DECT cordless telephone technology, using dedicated frequencies (1880-1920 MHz) and supporting both voice and packet data with 70-600 meter range depending on indoor or outdoor use.

MS/TP operates over RS-485 wired pairs and is used in building automation; it differs from wireless technologies by being mains-powered with no hidden node problem and support for large payloads without fragmentation. NFC enables secure contactless transfer at very short range (10 cm or less) and is useful for access control and secure healthcare applications. PLC (Power Line Communication) uses existing electrical wiring as the transmission medium in multiple variants: IEEE 1901 for broadband (200 Mbps), IEEE 1901.1 for medium frequency (10 Mbps), and IEEE 1901.2 and G3-PLC for narrowband (200-234 kbps). Each technology has different tradeoffs in topology support, mobility, latency, buffering needs, and implementation complexity.
sections.plainLanguage: Small devices can talk wirelessly through radio, Bluetooth, Z-Wave, and power lines, or by wire using building automation cables. Each method works differently, so IPv6 has to be tweaked for each one.

sections.title: Guidelines for Adopting 6lo in New Technologies
sections.content:
When adapting 6LoWPAN to a new link-layer technology, deployments must address several design decisions. Addressing determines how IPv6 addresses are formed from link-layer addresses and whether privacy considerations (such as address tracking) are handled. MTU and fragmentation decisions depend on whether the link layer handles large packets; some link layers now support fragmentation, eliminating the need for 6LoWPAN layer fragmentation. Mesh versus routing choices select between layer-2 mesh forwarding ("mesh-under") or layer-3 routing ("route-over"), with different implications for latency, complexity, and multi-hop reliability.

Address assignment relies on 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery, which optimizes IPv6's Neighbor Discovery for low-power networks by using unicast instead of multicast for address resolution and routing advertisements. Header compression is essential, reducing large IPv6 and transport-layer headers to just a few bytes. Security must be addressed at multiple levels: link-layer encryption, network-layer protocols like IPsec or DTLS, and physical-layer considerations like NFC's intrinsic short-range security. Broadcast avoidance reduces multicast traffic that translates into broadcast at the link layer, since broadcast consumes power in idle listening mode.
sections.plainLanguage: When engineers design IPv6 for a new kind of tiny gadget, they decide: How do we name the devices? Do we break big messages into pieces? Do the gadgets talk to each other directly or through a main router? How do we keep secrets?

sections.title: Real-World Deployment Examples
sections.content:
Wi-SUN (Wireless Smart Ubiquitous Network) is based on IEEE 802.15.4g and deploys in mesh topology using RPL routing for smart utility networks and smart city applications, including outdoor wide-area field area networks. Thread is an IPv6-based stack for smart home IEEE 802.15.4 mesh networks using 6LoWPAN header compression, mesh-under forwarding with distance-vector routing, and efficient end-to-end fragmentation. G3-PLC is a narrowband power line communication technology based on ITU-T G.9903, deployed in many countries for smart grid applications, supporting multi-hop mesh topology and using RPL routing for highly reliable long-range communication.

Netricity is the HomePlug Alliance program for IEEE 1901.2 low-frequency narrowband PLC, also used in smart grid and smart city applications. These deployments show that 6lo has enabled IPv6 to work reliably across diverse link-layer technologies, supporting applications from smart metering to advanced metering infrastructure to demand response in utility grids. Each deployment adapts the core 6LoWPAN techniques to its specific link-layer characteristics while maintaining the common IPv6 foundation.
sections.plainLanguage: Real systems using 6lo today include WiFi networks for power companies reading meters wirelessly, Bluetooth meshes in smart homes, and electricity meters that talk through power lines. All of them use the same basic IPv6 over tiny packets idea.

sections.title: Application Domains and Use Cases
sections.content:
6lo enables diverse applications across multiple domains. Smart homes use Z-Wave and Bluetooth LE to control lights, thermostats, and locks wirelessly with minimal installation cost and low power consumption. Wearable health monitoring uses Bluetooth LE to connect smartwatches and body sensors to phones, which relay data to cloud healthcare services. Building automation uses MS/TP (6LoBAC) to connect HVAC, lighting, and access control systems via existing twisted-pair wiring, enabling co-existence with legacy BACnet systems. Smart metering uses DECT-ULE, Z-Wave, and PLC to enable utility companies to read electricity and gas meters remotely without technician visits.

Smart grids use PLC in multiple variants for advanced metering infrastructure (AMI), demand response, distribution automation, and grid monitoring. Secure healthcare transfer uses NFC to transfer sensitive patient data with minimal risk of eavesdropping due to NFC's short 10-centimeter range. Emergency services use wireless communication to coordinate first responders and transmit vital signs data from patients. These diverse applications demonstrate that 6lo, once initially designed for IEEE 802.15.4, has become the enabling foundation for IPv6 in the broader Internet of Things ecosystem.
sections.plainLanguage: 6lo powers smart homes, fitness watches, building control, power meter reading, electricity grids, medical data transfer, and emergency response—basically any place where tiny devices need to join the Internet.
